content.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given daily stock prices, find the maximum profit achievable with AT MOST two transactions (a transaction is one buy followed by one sell; a new buy can only happen after the previous sell).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","prices array"],["Output","Maximum achievable profit using at most two transactions"],["Key Insight","Track four running profit states in a single pass: after the first buy, after the first sell, after the second buy, after the second sell"],["Constraints","Up to 10^5 days"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"At most k transactions\" (here, k=2, a small fixed number)","A finite-state DP tracking a small, fixed number of running \"best profit so far\" states, one pair of buy/sell per allowed transaction, all updated together in a single linear pass"]]}

blocks.text: With at most two transactions allowed, four running quantities fully capture every relevant possibility at each day: the best profit achievable if currently holding after a FIRST buy, the best profit after completing a FIRST sell, the best profit after a SECOND buy (using proceeds from the first sell), and the best profit after a SECOND sell. Each of these updates using the PREVIOUS day's values of the state just before it in this chain.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tracking Best-Case Profit Through Two Sequential Trades, Updated Daily
blocks.text: Picture a trader allowed at most two separate buy-then-sell trades, tracking four running best-profit figures day by day: after a first purchase, after cashing out the first trade, after reinvesting into a second purchase, and after cashing out the second trade, each depending on the previous stage's best value from the day before.

blocks.caption: Four running states (buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2), each updated once per day from the previous day's values

blocks.text: Maximum profit = 6 (buy at 0, sell at 3, then buy at 1, sell at 4).
Maximum profit = 4 (a single transaction, buy at 1, sell at 5, is already optimal, since a second transaction offers nothing extra here).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: buy1 tracks the best (most negative cost, i.e., highest achievable) profit if a first share is currently held, updated as max(buy1, -price) (buying today, or continuing to hold from a better earlier buy).

Observation 2: sell1 tracks the best profit after completing exactly one sell, updated as max(sell1, buy1 + price) (selling today using the best first-buy so far, or keeping a previous sell).

Observation 3: buy2 tracks the best profit if a SECOND share is currently held, funded using proceeds from having ALREADY completed the first sell, updated as max(buy2, sell1 - price).

Observation 4: sell2 tracks the best profit after completing a second sell, updated as max(sell2, buy2 + price), and this is the final answer, since ending with an unsold share is never better than having already cashed out when prices are fully known in advance.
This leads to four rolling variables (buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2), each updated once per day in that exact dependency order.
Conceptually, try every pair of non-overlapping buy-sell interval combinations directly, computing the total profit for each combination and keeping the best.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every pair of transaction intervals directly implements the definition of "at most two transactions" literally.
This costs O(n to the 4th power) or worse, utterly infeasible for up to 10^5 days; four rolling variables updated in one linear pass solve this in O(n) instead.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n to the 4th power) or worse, trying every pair of intervals.
Space: O(1) extra per candidate pair checked.
Limitation: four rolling variables, updated together in dependency order each day, capture the same information in a single O(n) pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Initialize buy1 and buy2 to negative infinity (no shares held yet), sell1 and sell2 to 0 (no profit yet). For each day's price, update IN THIS EXACT ORDER: buy1 = max(buy1, -price); sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + price); buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - price); sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + price). Updating in this order (buy1, then sell1, then buy2, then sell2) ensures each uses the CORRECT, appropriately timed value of the state it depends on within the same day's pass. The final answer is sell2.
Use four rolling variables, updated in dependency order (buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2) once per day.

codes.python:
def max_profit(prices):
    buy1 = buy2 = float('-inf')
    sell1 = sell2 = 0
    for price in prices:
        buy1 = max(buy1, -price)                             # best cost of the first buy
        sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + price)                       # best profit after the first sell
        buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - price)                          # best net cost of the second buy
        sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + price)                           # best profit after the second sell
    return sell2

blocks.text: Updating the four states IN ORDER (buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2) within the SAME day's pass correctly threads dependencies: sell1's update uses the value of buy1 that ALREADY reflects today's price (allowing a same-day buy-then-sell, which is valid since both operations use today's single price value consistently), and similarly buy2 correctly builds on sell1, and sell2 on buy2, all within one single linear scan, without ever needing to consider explicit transaction intervals.

blocks.text: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III generalizes the single-transaction stock problem to a small, fixed chain of states, each depending cleanly on the one before it.

items: Updating the four states in the WRONG order (for instance, computing buy2 before sell1 has been updated for the current day), breaking the intended same-day dependency chain.
Forgetting that ending in a "buy" state (holding an unsold share) is never optimal when all prices are known in advance, so the answer is always sell2, not a maximum involving buy2.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "at most k transactions" with a small fixed k, think: a chain of 2k rolling state variables, updated together in dependency order each day.

items: How would you generalize this to "at most k transactions" for an arbitrary k, using an array of 2k rolling variables or a small DP table instead of exactly four named variables?
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV, the direct generalization of this exact technique to an arbitrary transaction limit k.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force interval-pair search costs O(n^4) or worse; the four-rolling-variable approach costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: a small, fixed chain of rolling state variables, each updated in dependency order within a single pass.
Core Idea: track buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2, updating each once per day using the appropriately ordered previous states.
Time: O(n^4) or worse for the brute force, O(n) for the rolling-variable approach.
Space: O(1) extra per candidate pair for the brute force, O(1) extra overall for the rolling-variable approach.
Most Important Observation: updating states in the correct dependency order within the same pass allows valid same-day chaining.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately tricky hard-tier DP problem.
One line memory trick: buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2, updated in that exact order.
